Listening to the Data

Astronomers often examine measurements as points, curves, or colors on a screen, a university research team[1] also converts some measurements into sound. This process, called sonification, assigns audible features to numerical values. During an early demonstration, a listener noticed a brief cluster of high notes that was easy to overlook as a narrow spike on the projected graph.[2] The observation showed the team that listening could reveal patterns deserving closer visual inspection.

To build a sonification, the researchers first decide which relationships matter. Time may move from left to right on a graph and forward through a recording. A rising measurement might produce a higher pitch, while a stronger signal controls volume. The team maps these features—with rules, that remain[3] consistent throughout a recording. Consistency allows a listener to recognize good[4] changes without memorizing every value. After selecting a dataset, the sounds are tested by the researchers with listeners before revising the mapping.[5]

Several measurements can change at once. In addition,[6] the team avoids assigning a separate instrument to every column of data. Too many simultaneous sounds can conceal the pattern they are meant to express. Instead, the researchers choose three primary features; pitch for frequency, volume for intensity, and duration for the length of an event[7]. This limited musical vocabulary helps listeners translate[8] a complicated table into a sequence they can compare over time.

One recording represents repeated pulses from a distant object with evenly spaced tones; a slight delay appears as one tone arriving later than expected. Another turns changes in a star's brightness into a slow rise and fall of pitch. Neither recording replaces the original measurements. Researchers return to the numbers to test any pattern they hear. The team's guiding principle is concise: “Sound is not an answer added to the data; it is another route into the question.”[9] By making numerical relationships available to both sight and hearing, sonification expands how researchers can notice, compare, and investigate them.[10]
